MR. LOW    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN VANCOUVER "SUN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My attention has been called to a column on page 4 of the Vancouver Sun, dated December 8, written by one Elmore Philpott, and in that column he wrote:
Hence it would appear that the Social Credit party may be getting ready to make itself the deliberate and vocal champion of McCarthyism in Canada.
My question of privilege is this: The writer of the column from which this sentence was taken tries to make it appear that the Social Credit movement is making ready to champion McCarthyism in Canada. In this, the columnist Elmore Philpott is just as far off base as he has been in many of his wild speculations of late years. I want to make it clear to him and all others in Canada that the Social Credit movement, of which I have the honour to be the spokesman, is not now championing McCarthyism in Canada, and is not getting ready to do so in the future. I thought I had made that abundantly clear when I said in this chamber on November 25: "I should like to make it definitely known that I feel it is irresponsible conduct on the part of any Canadian to try to butt into their (United States') affairs."
Mr. Speaker, we have always urged, and we do now strongly urge, that every effort be made to keep communists and communist
sympathizers out of government departments and our vital industries. But when inquiries are instituted for screening or for other security purposes in Canada, we strongly urge that they be conducted under the unabridged rule of law; that great care be taken to ensure that men are not found guilty merely by association; and that the rights and freedoms of individual Canadians be fully respected and the dignity of our courts and legal processes be most carefully safeguarded.

Hon. members may recall that when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was speaking on the speech from the throne on November 16 he referred to the bill to revise the Criminal Code which received first reading on that day. At that time the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked

Criminal Code
whether it would be possible to have printed and made available to members the findings of the special committee of the last house, and stated further that it would go a long way toward doing away with the necessity of convening another special committee if those recommendations could be made available.
I understand that the queen's printer has available about 40 sets of the minutes and proceedings of the special committee of this house and about 85 sets of the minutes and proceedings of the banking and commerce committee to which the bill was referred last year in the other place. These quantities are obviously not sufficient to enable every hon. member to have a set of the proceedings of both committees. The cost of reprinting these proceedings, which run to over 400 pages, would be about $2,000. I would suggest that it might be sufficient if the available sets were distributed proportionately among the various groups in this house. On the other hand, it would appear to be desirable that every hon. member should have in his hands the report of the royal commission on the Criminal Code and should also have an opportunity to peruse the three reports of the special committee of this house that examined the bill in detail at the last session.
For that reason, sir, I would like to move, seconded by my hon. colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), that:
One thousand copies in English and 250 copies in French be printed of the report of the royal commission on the revision of the Criminal Code and of the three reports of the special committee of this house appointed to examine the bill and that in connection therewith the operation of standing order 64 be suspended.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MOTION TO PRINT REPORTS OF ROYAL COMMISSION AND SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask one question. In view of the inference in this motion that it is desirable for us to have this material in our hands, is it the intention of the minister to ask the house to proceed with the debate on second reading of the Criminal Code before we have that material?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION TO PRINT REPORTS OF ROYAL COMMISSION AND SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The answer to my hon. friend's question is yes. I think perhaps I should supplement that answer with a few words of explanation. The bill revising and consolidating the Canadian criminal law, which runs to over 756 sections, deals with a number of matters each one of which has a principle of its own: for example, the principle relating to the law on sedition, or to the law on murder, or to fraud. The suggestion which I propose to make to hon. members on the second reading of the Criminal Code bill is that we should treat as the principle of the second reading just the question as to whether, when a statute has been on the law

books of our country for over 60 years, the time has now come that it should be consolidated.
I should then like to suggest to hon. members that we could discuss the principle of the individual clauses or groups of clauses dealing with the various crimes when we have the bill in committee of the whole and when it will be possible to deal with those clauses in a much more orderly manner. Otherwise we would have on second reading of the bill a debate which might embrace the simultaneous discussion of a large number of principles which possess little relationship to one another except that they are all defined as crimes in a single criminal code.

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ON STANDARDIZATION OF SMALL ARMS AMMUNITION

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ON STANDARDIZATION OF SMALL ARMS AMMUNITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the house that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has today announced in Paris, on behalf of the North Atlantic council, that agreement has been reached by Belgium, Canada, France, the United Kingdom and the United States on the very important matter of standardization of small arms ammunition.
These five countries have agreed, as the result of extensive tests over a two-year period of close co-operation, to adopt as standard small arms ammunition the new 7-62 millimetre light-weight cartridge.
These tests have shown conclusively that there is no significant difference in the performance of rounds which were tested or examined of the 7 millimetre round, which in the English system is known as -280 calibre, and the 7-62 millimetre round which in the English system is known as -30 calibre. Decision to adopt the 7-62 millimetre round was based primarily on the over-all problem of retooling requirements and weapons production facilities of each country concerned. Since adoption of either the 7-62 millimetre or 7 millimetre cartridge would necessitate retooling by Canada and the United Kingdom, and adoption of the 7 millimetre would require retooling by all five countries, it was agreed that the most advanced 7-62 millimetre ammunition will be adopted as standard.
The five nations who co-operated in the solution of this problem jointly invited the other NATO nations to adopt it.

The successful outcome of the joint effort of the nations concerned is of special importance to Canada in view of our close relationship with the armed forces and supply systems of Great Britain on the one hand and the United States on the other.
It will be, I believe, a source of great satisfaction to members of this house and to Canadians generally that the important result which has just been achieved has been due in no small measure to the initiative and persistence of our own Minister of National Defence. The fact that he was asked to make the announcement in Paris on behalf of NATO was, I believe, recognition by the council of his important contribution to the solution of this difficult problem.
It is understood that troop trials by NATO countries of light-weight automatic rifles to use the new ammunition will commence relatively soon.
For Canadian troop trials, the Canadian army has ordered from Fabrique Nationale, Belgium, a number of new light-weight automatic rifles of a Belgian design, which will fire the new ammunition.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ON STANDARDIZATION OF SMALL ARMS AMMUNITION
speechtext: I should like to ask the Associate Minister of National Defence to say a further word or two with respect to the statement he has just made. Will he let us know whether the 7 [DOT] 6 millimetre is the type which was recently used by the Belgians and, I believe, adopted or recommended by the British, or whether it conforms to the type which was being advocated by the United States?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ON STANDARDIZATION OF SMALL ARMS AMMUNITION
speechtext: I am not sure on either count. The round adopted has been the subject of a good deal of research, discussion and consideration for two years. It is the ultimate result of lall these discussions in which no doubt the Belgian, American and other types were considered. I cannot therefore answer unequivocally the hon. gentleman's question.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ON STANDARDIZATION OF SMALL ARMS AMMUNITION

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. In the interests of the people in the coal mining industry, can the minister, either today or some time before the Christmas recess, make a statement to the house regarding the progress of the experiment by his department into the development of a coal-burning gas turbine?

speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON EXPERIMENTAL GAS TURBINE ENGINE
speechtext:
I wish to thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, for the past three years, has been sponsoring the design and construction of an experimental coalburning gas turbine by the gas dynamics laboratory of McGill University. The purpose of the unit is to carry out research into the
Inquiries of the Ministry problems of using coal as a fuel for a gas turbine engine with a view to the propulsion of locomotives or the production of electric power.
The experimental engine, which includes new features designed to make the use of coal practical, was recently completed and the test program begun. On November 27, after preliminary runs using oil, the first test of coal was made and was satisfactory. This was the first run of an exhaust-heated turbine engine in the world, and the third time that power has been produced from coal in a gas turbine, the first and second occasions having been tests of other types of units in the United Kingdom and United States of America. The distinctive feature of the exhaust-heated turbine engine is the heat exchangers. With these exchangers, no fly ash or other products of the combustion of coal can foul the turbine blades.
It is anticipated that the second stage of the research program to be carried out on this plant will extend over some two years. From the point of view of convenience of experimental and research work, the plant is one of the best equipped gas turbines in the world.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, December 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 29, to amend the Customs Act-Mr. McCann- Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On section 1-Value for duty where market price has declined.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, enough was said in the debate on second reading of this measure to have indicated that the house in committee of the whole would wish to examine quite closely the detailed provisions of this short bill. As I have some observations to make about the particular language of the bill, may I at the outset attempt to put in perspective the observations I should like to make in that regard.
I wish to make it abundantly clear again that we of the official opposition support the bill as a measure designed to grapple with the problem of dumping. Dumping is a fact. Dumping has been going on in this country at an increasing rate, particularly during the past two years and even more particularly during the past year. We say that something effective must be done to grapple with this problem which has been allowed to reach very serious proportions as a result of the government's inaction. Therefore, what we of the official opposition seek in a measure of this kind is that it should be clear, effective and capable of fair and adequate enforcement. It is by these standards, Mr. Chairman, that we approach the detailed consideration of the terms of this bill in this committee.
Sir, the example given by the minister concerning textile imports was, as he pointed out, not an exclusive enumeration of the articles which are being dumped into Canada from the United States. He stated that he was mentioning textiles as an example. It is quite true that textiles are a striking example to illustrate the dumping of United States products into Canada today. But, sir, it would be, in my submission, unwise to limit or restrict the provisions of this bill in the way in which the bill is restricted in its terms now.
I should like to remind the committee that this short bill purports to amend section 35 of the Customs Act. Section 35 of the Customs Act relates to the dumping of goods. There is no restriction now in the terms of section 35 in relation to the nature or definition of goods. Goods are defined in the

interpretation section of the Customs Act, section 2, in rather broad terms. Subsection (j) provides:
"goods" means goods, wares and merchandise or movable effects of any kind, including vehicles, horses, cattle and other animals;
There we have an interpretation that is clear, one which has been defined by statute. This enables those charged with enforcement and interpretation of the act to have a clear statutory definition of long standing to guide them in their interpretation of the act. But, sir, this bill proposes to amend section 35 by the introduction of certain new provisions limited, if you iplease, to "manufactured goods". Why should there be a limitation, Mr. Chairman? If the type of legislation with which we are dealing is sound, why should it be so restricted in its application?
Speaking last Thursday on second reading, I sought to suggest that if you limit it in this way, if you confine this new anti-dumping provision to what are called in this bill "manufactured goods", I am quite certain that those in the United States who find it profitable today to dump their products in Canada are not going to find it beyond their ingenuity to devise ways of circumventing a narrow definition of this kind. Bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, that the words "manufactured goods" are not defined in the act. The word "manufactured" is not defined in the act. The introduction of a provision of this kind is necessarily going to create difficulties and complexities for those who are charged with the problem of interpretation and enforcement at the various customs points of entry from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It would be far better for us not to introduce restrictive language of this kind but to use the terms employed in section 35, the parent section which is being amended by this bill.
In this way it would lie within the power of the government to apply this measure wherever or to any product where dumping exists, and that is in keeping with the principle and purpose of the entire section. Now, that is my first observation, Mr. Chairman, about the restrictions in this bill which it seems to me are unwise and which are going to create difficulties and complexities for those charged with the interpretation and enforcement of the provision.
It is not out of place now to call attention to another restriction in this bill which I feel is unwise, and that is the restriction which purports to confine the cause of dumping to only two cases. The bill uses these words:
... as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period, . . .

Then, the operative words go on:
, . . declined to levels that do not reflect in the opinion oi the minister their normal price, the value for duty shall be the amount determined and declared by the minister . . .
We are, I take it, in agreement or certainly should be, as to the necessity for passing effective legislation to deal with the kind of dumping that results from the action of United States manufacturers who, having arrived at the end of a season or the end of their run of goods, find it profitable to dump those goods in Canada as a purely salvage operation. This section applies only to goods at end of run or end of the season. These manufacturers have made their profit on their major run, and in the United States those runs are in huge quantities, the like of which we do not begin to manufacture in this country. The United States manufacturer does not wish to spoil his domestic market, so he prefers that these goods should be sent abroad to be disposed of there at a sacrifice or as salvage, for almost anything they will bring. He does not wish to hurt his domestic market in the United States for the next run of goods in the following season. It is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that Canada, being adjacent to the United States, is much favoured by the United States manufacturers under those conditions, and has become what was referred to on Friday as the "happy dumping ground". But the dumping which exists today is not necessarily confined to goods that are being sent here as a result of the advance of the season or the marketing periods. It is known that there are United States manufacturers who find it to their advantage to continue operations for a period even at a loss in order to maintain their staffs and their plant, to avoid the dislocations that go with shutdowns. In such a case, their operations cannot be described in those limited words, "the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period."
In my submission those words add nothing to the effectiveness of this measure, nor do they, I am sure, contribute anything toward allaying any of the fears expressed in the house, such as those voiced by the hon. member for Rosthern. In my submission they do nothing except to complicate the measure, and perhaps make it easy for some astute exporter in the United States to find a way around the limited terms of the amendment.
Now, why should we introduce such words as these, "as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period"? Surely in the face of the proven fact of dumping and the broad variety of forms it takes, as well as the extent to which it has grown in volume and in nature, it would be a serious mistake
Customs Act
for the house to narrow the effect of the bill by the type of definition I have read. Wherever prices of manufactured goods exported to this country have declined to levels that do not, in the opinion of the minister, reflect their normal price, then surely the minister, if this bill is sound-as we think it should be-and if it is properly phrased, should have the power to apply the provisions of the bill to prevent the dumping.
Then why, sir, should we narrow down the occasions giving rise to the decline of the price in question to a level where it does not in the opinion of the minister reflect the normal price? Mr. Chairman, if we are going to introduce restrictive words of that kind it will mean for those in this country who are charged with their enforcement and interpretation many complexities and difficulties. It will mean for Canadian importers problems in trying to understand the customs barriers they will have to consider. It means, I think, an opportunity for astute American exporters to find a way to overcome the effect of this measure.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that is not a situation we ought to make possible. If we eliminate the words, "as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period" then in my submission we are strengthening the hands of the minister to deal with this problem. We are not leaving loopholes to be circumvented by astute American exporters, so that they can avoid the restrictive terms of the measure and dump their products in Canada.
Speaking in the debate on second reading last Thursday evening I laid not a little stress on the problem of interpretation, and I make no apology for stressing the theme again today in relation to the words to which I have specially referred as they appear in section 1 of the bill.
It should be our objective in relation to legislation of this kind to make it as simple and as clear as possible, and to make it possible also for rulings to be given with speed and with uniformity, in all parts of Canada. That is the duty we owe not only to the Canadian importer and the American exporter but also to the officials of the Department of National Revenue as well. It is going to be no help in the problem with which we are seeking to deal simply to hold in a state of suspension rulings people seek, and seek properly, in relation to the terms upon which they can import into this country.
The concluding words of the section, under which the minister is called upon to follow a very complicated formula in deciding what

Customs Act
is the normal price of manufactured goods, is going to make it difficult enough to give uniform, clear and speedy interpretations to this section. Then, Mr. Chairman, let us go as far as we can in simplifying the measure and at the same time strengthen it against efforts which will certainly be made to get around its otherwise limited scope.
Again let me say to hon. members such as the hon. member for Rosthern, who spoke on this subject, that there is nothing in what I am suggesting now that need give rise to any fear on the part of anyone who shares the point of view he expressed. If the measure is sound we are simply seeking to make it clear, and simply making certain that it is as broad in its application as the parent section it seeks to amend, namely, section 35 of the Customs Act.
How far the government goes in relation to the price it sets will be of course the responsibility of the government. But, Mr. Chairman, surely every member in the chamber knows now that the problem exists, that it is a serious and an acute problem; and if we are going to undertake seriously to grapple with it, then let us not do it in complicated terms that are difficult of interpretation, and so narrow in the draftsmanship of the bill that they will only give rise to confusion and complexity, and leave gaps for people to circumvent the intent of parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with that object in view I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell):
That clause 1 of Bill 29 be amended by striking out of the proposed new section 35 (6) of the Customs Act, the following words:	The word
"manufactured", in line 8, and the words "as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period", in lines 9 and 10.
May I now read the section, including the amendments I have just proposed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit an interruption? Would he not prefer to move the amendment in two parts? I believe the government might be quite prepared to accept the first part, but might have some reservations about the second. If it is submitted in its present form the qualifications and objections would have to be urged against the motion to amend. On the other hand, if it is submitted in two parts the qualifications which apply only to the second part would not be urged against the first.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I readily accept the Prime Minister's suggestion. In view of what he has said I am quite prepared to move it in two parts. In view of what the Prime

Minister has said about the first part I shall not labour what will now become the first amendment.
Perhaps I might be permitted to read the section with the amendment, as I was about to do when he spoke. It would read in this way, with the two amendments:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, where the market price of any goods in the country of export lias declined to levels that do not reflect in the opinion of the minister their normal price, the value for duty shall be the amount determined and declared by the minister

And so on. I believe I have made clear the effect of the two proposals, and what I think would be helpful in the matter of interpretation and enforcement of the measure if these amendments were made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
By way of verification, perhaps I should read the amendment. The hon. member for Eglinton moves:
That clause 1 of Bill 29 be amended by striking out of the proposed new section 35 (6) of the Customs Act, the following word:	The word
"manufactured" in line 8.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I understood that the Prime Minister accepted the proposal made by the hon. member for Eglinton. To my mind that would be a very serious widening of the scope of what is proposed. The cutting out of the word "manufactured" leaves the department and the minister in the position where any goods may be dealt with. It seems to me that that is going pretty far and asks the house to accept a great deal, particularly those who probably feel as I do myself. While we wanted to do something that would prevent the dumping of certain goods that caused unemployment in the country, this goes far beyond what we think is required at the present time to meet an emergency situation.
There is no safeguard in the measure now before us regarding the length of time that this legislation will last. I have grave doubts myself as to the wisdom of making the measure as wide as the amendment proposes to do. Because of all the implications, it would be wise for the government to give the hon. member's amendment pretty serious consideration before the committee is asked to accept the widening of the measure in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
The moving of this amendment indicates exactly where we are headed. If you do this for manufacturers in order to protect their employees against temporary unemployment, then by what manner of reasoning can you say that you should not do it to protect farmers against fruits and

vegetables being dumped before our season comes in, and even when our season does come in, and underselling our farmers?
Ever since I have been a member of the house I have heard representatives of farming districts of Ontario and British Columbia pointing out that they were being exposed to unfair competition from fruits and vegetables grown in the United States; that the growers in the United States could not get rid of them, they were going to spoil, and they were dumping them in Canada for anything they could get for them. Something has been done to meet that situation; but I can easily see, Mr. Chairman, that if you do it for manufacturers you cannot deny it to anybody else, and ultimately you have it embedded in the law as a principle that if anyone in Canada, be he a manufacturer, a farmer or anybody else, comes along and says that he cannot meet competition from abroad for one reason or another, you must grant him this protection. If he comes along and says that he cannot meet the competition because of the end of the season, then you are going to help him out to prevent unemployment. An individual may say that on account of the fact that we live in a colder climate it is going to cost more to manufacture. Therefore, in certain seasons of the year, we must have a tariff of that kind. Reasons can be given for increasing the tariff, many different reasons. If you grant it for one reason, how are you going to draw the line and say you are not going to grant it for another reason? In other words, as I pointed out, this starts out by being emergency legislation. Unless it is definitely so regarded and stated, then of course industry begins to build up on the strength of this protection, and if at any time later on there is an attempt to change it, you have established the vested interest and it is very difficult to take away protection you have already given, and others begin to demand the same protection and the thing spreads and spreads.
The trouble in regard to this matter is this, and I think it is recognized by everybody. Our biggest market for our manufacturers of central Canada is after all the home market, which is growing in size, value and wealth. It is based upon the foundation of the primary producer being able to sell his products in the markets of the world where they cannot be protected, at a given price, and with that money they are able to buy the products of the rest of Canada.
If in your attempt to protect people against temporary emergencies you cause other countries to raise their tariffs against the
Customs Act
primary producers, you will destroy our purchasing power to the extent where you will have real unemployment. I suggest that if this is really emergency legislation it should not be extended in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton. This is emergency legislation to deal with a certain specific situation, and it should be definitely recognized in the legislation; it should be written right in the legislation that this is only for a definite period, say for one year, so that at the end of the year nobody can come along and say: We have built up our industry, or we have spent money, or we have expanded on the strength of this legislation, and now you are proposing to take it away. They should be put upon notice that this is in the nature of emergency legislation, and an attempt to see how the thing will work.
There is another reason why I suggest that this should be definitely made emergency legislation. One of the reasons has been shown by the amendment just moved. There is a thought on the part of the hon. member for Eglinton that this is permanent legislation; that it should be extended to everyone. This committee should be at great pains to make it clear that this is definitely not permanent legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: I remind the hon. member that he is speaking to the amendment of the hon. member for Eglinton, which removes the word "manufactured" from the clause. I suggest that his present discussion is a little far afield.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I thought I was dealing to some extent with the basic argument of the hon. member for Eglinton. His argument was that if this was a good thing for manufactured goods it was a good thing for everyone. I am suggesting, as I understand it, the reason why it applies only to manufactured goods. The reason is that it is passed to meet a definite situation that has developed in certain branches of manufacturing. I will bow to your ruling, of course, but I am suggesting that this is put through to apply to manufactured goods because of that emergency situation. Therefore there is less reason to apply it to everything. If you apply it to everything, then you have a situation where other industries besides manufacturing industries will feel that they have a right to take advantage of it, and if the thing does not work out it will be much harder to do away with it.
I suggest that it should not be widened, because it would make it much more difficult to repeal it if it does not work out properly. This is the point I wish to make, and I do

Customs Act
not think I am out of order, but if you rule I am I will not press the point. We are going to be engaged in negotiations in regard to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. If this is extended for one year we shall be engaged in negotiation. I submit that if we have this definitely as emergency legislation, restricted to meet the situation that we have before us, we shall be in a much better position to say to the United States and to the other countries that are putting on these different rulings that are interfering with trade and being so unfair to our producers: This is emergency legislation: our parliament dealt with it just for manufactured goods only. We want it understood that it is not our permanent attitude. If you people will negotiate with us in good faith, end those arbitrary rulings, and do everything you can to facilitate trade, this will apply only to manufactured goods and for a certain period of time. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, the amendment makes the situation worse even than the original bill, in my humble judgment, and I hope that the government, before this bill is reported out of committee, will have given some consideration to an amendment in the other direction making it quite clear that this legislation is going to be kept in force for a limited period only, until it can be seen whether it is going to do more good than harm.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the course of debate I think it has become clearly evident that this legislation will be supported in all parts of the house although some criticism has arisen regarding the wording of the bill.
As regards the matter of manufactured goods I think it is generally considered that the textile industry has been suffering to some extent in the past few months and the industry itself seems to feel this amendment would assist in providing employment for many employees throughout the country. In addition to that, the hon. member for Rosthern has referred to the group of citizens whom I have the honour to represent, namely, certain fruit and vegetables growers in the province of Ontario. I believe we grow in our part of the country just as fine a quality of fruit and vegetables as are grown in any other part of Canada. We take second place to no one.
The growers there have initiative, enterprise and ability to produce these commodities at prices as low as can be found anywhere, but we have found that, owing to recent advance in the period when these articles can be produced, there is a great flow of fresh fruits and vegetables as well as
[Mr. Tucker.l
processed fruits and vegetables coming into this country. In 1952 peaches were literally dumped into lake Ontario, and I would remind hon. members that peaches are a perishable product like all other fresh fruits and vegetables, and there is no possibility of carrying them over into another year.
I would like to feel that a definition of goods could be made to include fruits and vegetables and also processed fruits and vegetables, because our products are of fine quality, as fine a quality as can be purchased, and they are attractively packaged. I believe the public purchases these other products simply because they somehow got into Canada. I am not prepared to say they have been dumped in the market over the years or whether they would come within the technical definition of dumping. Possibly they do not, but I believe it has been difficult to prove where the articles have been dumped, technically speaking, in the market in the past few years.
However, a provision in this bill to include fruit and vegetables and processed fruit and vegetables would be a great benefit to those people I have the honour to represent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I was not surprised at the amendment suggested by the member for Eglinton calling for the deletion of the word "manufactured", but the Prime Minister really took me by surprise when he indicated that the government was prepared to accept that amendment. I do not think I need spend any time developing the argument against it because it has been outlined by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and also the member for Rosthern. Fundamentally, it seems to me that to accept this amendment is not only to broaden the terms of this alleged anti-dumping section but to move further in the direction of protection which can only mean sooner or later an increase in the cost of living in Canada.
I would strongly urge the Prime Minister and other members of the government to consider very carefully this question in all its implications before accepting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton.
There is another aspect of this question on which I wish to say something, but I think perhaps I had better reserve it until we get to a general discussion of the clause. Perhaps I may refer to it just in passing because it reinforces my opposition to this amendment. As I read the clause as it stands- and in my view it will be worse if the other amendment of the member for Eglinton were accepted-a great deal is left to the discretion of the minister. That in turn means the discretion of the people down in the department.

I will develop that later on when I think it is more in order, but I submit it now merely to indicate that this amendment is carrying what has been brought in as legislation against dumping, because particular industries are suffering, to protection of a nature and extent that we might expect from some party other than the party which across the years has claimed that it was loyal to the principles of free trade.
There is just one other comment I would like to make. I have quite a few documents and volumes on my desk but I do not happen to have a copy of the tariff act. However, if my memory serves me right there are sections in the tariff act dealing with seasonal importation of fruits and vegetables. Therefore, I suggest that any products other than manufactured goods which it is intended to cover by the amendment from the member for Eglinton are already covered. This amendment would take that principle much further. I was not surprised at the amendment. I will not be surprised at the heat of the debate it may produce in this house, but I do hope the Prime Minister and the government will think the matter over very seriously before they go so far as to agree to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps at this stage it might be of some help if I made a statement or at least made some comments with reference to the points that have already been raised. Everyone who has so far spoken in this debate is in favour of the principle of the bill. I have not heard any objection yet. Some arguments have been advanced with reference to the details of the bill which I think can quite easily be ironed out.
I want to state very definitely that we are not asking that the word "manufactured" be removed, but if this is the wish of the house we are quite ready to accept it.
With reference to the second amendment, which has not yet been put but which was indicated by the member for Eglinton, let me read the relevant section:
. . . where the market price of any manufactured goods in the country of export has, as a result of the advance of the season or the marketing period, declined to levels that do not reflect . . .
I suggest that that is more of a descriptive nature than anything else, because you will note it says very distinctly in the explanatory note what the purpose of the additional subsection is. and I quote:
... it is to supplement and to widen the law to provide a fair and reasonable basis of valuation . . .
The basis for a reasonable valuation would be determined by the conditions in the
Customs Act
country of export, as a result of the advance of the season or marketing period. That means the end of the line or the other reason which has previously been given.
With reference to the matter of protection accorded to the fruit and vegetable industry, may I say that it is already protected and has been for a number of years. Fresh fruits and vegetables were subject to a fixed valuation for duty purposes under section 43 of the Customs Act with the application of a dumping duty during the Canadian marketing season. That was the custom. As a result of the general agreement on tariffs and trade those fixed values were for 1950-as recently as that-translated into minimum seasonal specific duties. The specific rates and maximum periods during which they may be applied are contained in the Customs Tariff Act. These rates are intended to protect the grower during his marketing period which, of course, varies from year to year. In their application the department is guided as to the appropriate duties by advice which we receive from the Department of Agriculture. Let me give an example. Pears, which are normally subject to an ad valorem duty of 10 per cent the year round, may be subject to an alternative specific duty of one cent per pound for a period of fifteen weeks, in addition to the specific dumping duty which would apply if the selling price to the purchaser in Canada was less than the fair market value as sold for home consumption in the country of export.
I suggest to the committee that that is really good protection. Then we come along to what was spoken about here the other day by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, which is a great fruit growing country. If we have manufactured goods-and canned cherries must be classed as that-then that is another commodity which would be subject to exactly the same regulations as would obtain for other manufactured goods.
I thought I made the matter fairly clear in my reply to a question that was asked on December 8 by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). As reported at page 693 of Hansard he asked this question:
How far does the minister consider that the anti-dumping instructions given to customs officials yesterday can be effectively applied to industries other than the textile industry, which he mentioned, and also to other production including agricultural production?
The answer I gave was as follows:
I mentioned the textile industry specifically in my statement yesterday because, in recent weeks, we had been hearing more about the difficulties which this particular industry has been facing. It will be noted on reference to the bill that no specific mention is made of any particular commodity, and any industry which finds itself

Customs Act
suffering unfair competition in the same form as the textile industry would be in a position to receive the same relief from unfair competition.
I think that is sufficiently broad to include manufactured commodities other than textiles and they could get the same measure of protection. Mr. Chairman, I do not think there has been sufficient discussion in the house as to why the textile industry is perhaps in the position in which it finds itself. It is true that some of the manufactured articles under what might be termed, if you like, distress selling are sold in this country. But there is a misunderstanding as to what constitutes dumping. The fact that goods of the United States-and I am only taking those as an example-are sold in this country at prices less than the Canadian prices does not constitute dumping. Dumping is when they are sold at prices less than those at which they are offered for sale and are sold in the country of export and in the country where they are manufactured.
In this bill we propose to widen the period over which the average weighted price shall be taken. It is not true-and that statement has been made, although I do not know whether it was in the House of Commons or not-that we have accepted the invoice of one particular sale as indicating the price at which those commodities were sold in the country of export. That is not the case. These invoices are examined. Appraisal is made of the goods-and that has been the practice throughout the years with reference to it-to attempt to find out whether or not they have been sold at a fair market value in their own country and whether the price at which they were invoiced into Canada was less than the fair market value.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: For what period? I ask that just for clarification.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
For a reasonable period and in respect of representative quantities of the goods. We would not on any occasion take one single isolated sale, without investigation, and say that is the fair market value of those goods in the country.
Then of course when the invoice is revised, the duty and taxes are added onto the price on the invoice, plus the amount that is added which constitutes the dump. The tax and the duties are added, and the dump is placed on that basis.
I do not know that there is need for any further explanation with reference to this matter. I think the hon. member for Rosthern introduced the matter of administrative difficulties. Of course there are going to be administrative difficulties. There cannot help being administrative difficulties with

regard to such a complicated subject as the matter of appraisal of thousands of articles every day across the country. As a result of our investigations which we have been carrying on and which we will continue to carry on with an augmented staff of people specially trained, I believe that we shall be able to arrive at what are the selling prices of the different manufactured commodities in the United States. They will centre from Ottawa. With reference to textiles, they will go into the principal marketing places where textiles are marketed; that is mostly in New York city, in the textile area in the New England states, in the middle west, in Chicago and in the southern states. By that method I believe we can get at a fair valuation of out-of-season goods and end-of-the-line goods so that we shall be able to give a fair measure of protection. It is protection. There is no getting away from that fact. But it is protection in a different manner from that of raising the tariff.
The hon. gentleman opposite, who, I see, is rather amused about that statement, wanted to know something about the policy of this party and of this government with reference to trade matters. He complained that we were a mongrel concoction of free traders and all the rest of it. They were not particularly dignified terms to be used in the House of Commons. There is another explanation for the word "mongrel" than the one he probably wanted to give it. We in this party and in this government stand for freer trade when that means expanding trade. That has been our policy for years and that will continue to be the policy of the Liberal party.
I do not think there will be anything to be gained by deleting the word "manufactured"; but, as I said, if that is the wish of the committee we are prepared to accept it. Perhaps I should not say we are prepared to accept it but rather that we are prepared to let the matter go to the committee and if it turns out that the word is deleted, we will administer the law on that basis. I do not think that it would be on a much, if any, different basis from what it will be with the word before the word "goods".

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: That is not what the Prime Minister said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
May I just say a word in order to try to explain to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there need be no surprise at the suggestion I made to the hon. member for Eglinton, that if he separated his amendments and presented the one for the deletion of the word "manufactured" first, we would have nothing to say

against it. That is what surprised the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I do not think there should be any surprise. When the bill was drafted we considered that the position of the Canadian producer of seasonal goods, vegetables or fruits, was sufficiently protected by the provisions already included in the tariff act. But there was nothing that could take care of what did amount in our opinion to actual dumping, that is to say, selling in this market, at prices that were not the normal prices of the goods sold, end of line or out of season goods. We thought that did amount to what most people would regard as dumping.
Of course people do not all agree as to what amounts to dumping and what does not amount to dumping. There are many who have tried to impress upon me that it is dumping for certain manufacturers to have lines that sell regularly at lower prices than those at which similar lines can be manufactured here in Canada. If that is the regular normal price for the selling of those lines in the country from which they are exported, the government does not regard that as dumping. But if a large percentage of a certain line is sold at a profitable price and the remainder is then sold for anything that can be got for it, and that price happens to be much lower than the normal price, that is regarded as in fact dumping and is regarded as something that our established industries in Canada do not have to put up with from the point of view of fair trade practices.
The bill was designed to meet that position. It was suggested that this was something that was being done merely for the manufacturers. We do not want the impression created in the minds of the public that we favour any class of the population, and that is why, if it should be felt in the house that the inclusion of the word "manufactured" in the bill indicates that there is a preference being shown for a certain class of Canadian citizen, we have no objection to that word being deleted. I do not think it will make any difference whatsoever in the application of the act. I feel confident that the growers will prefer their seasonal duties to any attempt to treat as dumping the selling at the end of the season of fruits or vegetables produced in the country to the south of us before our season is in full swing. I think they will prefer to know in advance that they are going to have, while our season is in full swing, the protective duties that are provided already in the tariff act.
But we do not want them to get the impression, because the word "manufactured" may be in this legislation, that they are being discriminated against. I do not think it is
Customs Act
going to make any difference whatsoever. 1 am quite prepared to argue at all times that they are not being discriminated against and that the word "manufactured" here is descriptive of the situation we have in mind because we do not have a seasonal situation that requires to be taken care of. But it does not help or hinder in -the application of this disposition that we envisage to have the word "manufactured" there or not to have it there. If there are hon. members who feel that there might be some cases where this provision should apply which would not be properly described as manufactured goods, and the minister in fact could be convinced that there were goods that could not be described as manufactured goods to which this situation would apply, then there is no objection on our part to leaving that open. But I do not see that there are any others who would be affected as the result of the advance of the season or of the marketing period bringing about selling at abnormal prices.
Once again, if prices though low are the prices at which these goods normally sell in the country of export, there is no intention to regard that as dumping because in our opinion it would not be dumping. But in recent years the situation with respect to end of season or end of line goods has worsened so far as our Canadian manufacturers are concerned, because formerly, when these surplus goods could be sold all over the world by the United States producers, there was no concentrating on getting them into the Canadian market. Under present currency conditions, however, the only market where they can get the kind of money for these sacrifice sales that they want to receive is the Canadian market. For that reason there have been greater efforts to get these end of season and end of marketing period goods disposed of in the Canadian market than heretofore, because this is the only market where they can get dollars.
That does not seem to us to create the kind of competition to which our regular Canadian producers have to submit. With respect to the possibility of some of them not being manufacturers, the growers are already taken care of by the seasonal duties. Nevertheless we would not object to removing the word "manufactured" because we do not want to give the impression that this is being done as a favour for any special group of Canadian producers.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I appreciate what the Prime Minister has said, but what I am getting at is this. When an act of this description is examined by the courts it is, as we are so often told in the house, the letter of the law that governs, the written word, rather than the intention of parliament in the passing of

Customs Act
the legislation. The Prime Minister and the Minister of National Revenue are perfectly right when they tell us that the fruit and vegetable growers are protected for a certain length of time, the length of time that they require to be protected against unfair competition from another country, whether it is the United States, Mexico, the West Indies or any other country. To that extent, because of the time limit, the special tariff legislation is restrictive.
As I understand it, what we are doing here is endeavouring to meet an emergency situation, and my objection to cutting out the word "manufactured" is that it broadens the effect of the legislation unnecessarily. It would be no longer restrictive in the sense that we were prepared to accept it to meet the emergency situation. I noted that the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Revenue said that the house could decide this question. I think that is a very good suggestion, and since an amendment has been moved I think what we should do is have a standing vote to see what hon. members desire.
For my part I want to confine this legislation to as narrow a field as possible because I do not like the principle which may be involved in giving additional protection. The other point that I do not like about the legislation is the one the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised a short time ago, namely, that it leaves the matter entirely in the hands of the minister. I am not criticizing the present minister when I say this, but so frequently on this side of the house we have criticized various acts that have come before us on the ground that certain matters were left to the particular minister.
Here we have a suggested widening of an act under which we accept the principle that the minister may decide in this emergency situation, and I think it would be in the best interests of the whole house if we stuck to the restricted area which was intended to be covered by this legislation when it was introduced. That is what I think and, as I say, the growers of fruit and vegetables are protected now by the tariff act which, if adequately administered should afford them the seasonal protection they may need. I believe the Canadian people would be much more satisfied if parliament made this provision as restrictive as possible to meet an emergency situation which we all admit does exist.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
In supporting this amendment, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I believe I have on my desk an example of the type of evasion which can be practised

by those people who are always looking for an opportunity to evade the regulations of the customs department. I have here a sample of a nylon stocking which is imported into this country in what is known as a semifinished state. This item enters the country as flat grey goods because it is not finished. This results in a price differential which is most unfavourable to the manufacturers of like products in this country.
Since it comes in as flat grey goods, I am given to understand that the ad valorem duty is 15 per cent and the specific duty 3 cents a pound. Since this article does not weigh very much you can put a good many into a pound. The finished product enters the country from the United States at a duty of 17-5 per cent ad valorem and a specific duty of 75 cents per dozen.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is a good example of the type of thing we can expect unless we remove from this bill the word "manufactured". Even with the word omitted there will undoubtedly be some evasions. I feel that not only nylon hosiery but a good many manufactured articles can be imported under just such a regulation or through just such loopholes and result in damage to an industry which has already suffered greatly in the last few years.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Are the goods in that form sold cheaper in Canada than they are in the United States?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: They are not sold in this form in Canada. They are finished here. They are seamed and dyed here.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Does the manufacturer in Canada get them in that form, if he wishes to complete the manufacture, at the same price as the United States manufacturer doing an analogous job in the United States?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: I do not think I follow the hon. member. Would he explain?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: I am trying to find out if there is any dumping. The only way in which there could be any dumping would be if the firm in the United States made an article of this description to be finished in a United States factory or in a Canadian factory, and if there were a lower price paid by the Canadian manufacturer who finishes the product in Canada.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot answer that question. I do know that this provides an opportunity for importation into

this country, not only at the end of season but at any time when the plant in question desires to keep the employees busy. The plant is at liberty to keep running and throw the production into this country because it is known there would be a market here for the product. These people evade the regulations of our Customs Act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: The example mentioned really is not relevant to this amendment of the Customs Act, in my judgment. I think it is a tariff item. What the hon. member desires is a change in the tariff which would afford more protection on that item. In this case the inducement to bring the product over in that state is to afford work to Canadian people to finish the product. It is true it is not very much, but that is the principle behind it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must take exception to that statement. After all, there is a lot more work for Canadian workmen in manufacturing the whole stocking than there is in simply sewing it up and dyeing it. The plant in Canada does not even need to have knitting machinery to finish the stocking. It can be finished in the plant without any knitting machinery whatever. As a matter of fact, what I had intended to point out was that this is an example of the type of evasion which can result unless we plug some of these loopholes.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
It is indeed a pleasure for me to rise at this time, Mr. Chairman, to do something a little bit different from some of the other hon. members in the house. I am going to thank the government, on behalf of the fruit and vegetable growers of British Columbia, for allowing this bill to be amended by striking out the word "manufactured". I did have an amendment prepared along the same lines to delete the word "manufactured" from the bill.
Some questions have been asked as to why we should ask for this when the matter has apparently been covered so well in the act. I think that the latter part of this amendment to the bill which reads-
. . . the average price, weighted as to quantity, at which the like or similar goods were sold for consumption in the country of export during a reasonable period, not exceeding six months, immediately preceding the date of shipment of the goods to Canada-
-is the main reason for desiring to have the word "manufactured" deleted from this bill. In this way we would be sure that all the provisions of the amendment would apply to fruit and vegetables. Again, on behalf of the fruit and vegetable growers of British Columbia, I should like to commend the government for the decision to delete the word "manufactured" from this bill.
Customs Act

speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister if he has any information as to the quantities of textiles which have been imported into Canada during the past two years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: The total imports of fibres, textiles and textile products from the United States-of course, we do get textiles from other countries-for eight months in 1952 amounted to $121,109,373; in 1953, for eight months, it was $16 million greater, making a total of $137,981,961.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I want to take a very few minutes to go on record as supporting the suggestions made here by the hon. member for Rosthern. I feel as he does, that this is a matter that must be dealt with very carefully. In my opinion we have had examples already in this house of the pressure that might be brought to bear, after this regulation goes into effect, from groups who are looking for protection. Many people may feel that the contrary is true, but that is a matter of opinion, depending upon whether one believes in freer trade or protection.
I believe that this measure should be considered as emergency legislation. Again I agree with the member for Rosthern when he suggests that some time limit should be put in this legislation so that we can come back and deal with it again. At that time we would know how it had been dealt with, and we could form our own opinion as to whether or not the provision should be continued. I want to give one example of an experience of my own with dumping duties. This was in the thirties. In the county of Charlotte, we use hundreds of thousands of gallons of edible oils every year in the canning industry. Between 1930 and 1935 we were importing all those oils from Great Britain. It was cottonseed oil. The government sitting here in Ottawa at that time was that of a party which has always been a great believer in doing everything we can for Great Britain. The oil was coming to this country free of duty, and continued in that way for a couple of years.
Then, the first thing we knew, a gentleman from the Department of National Revenue came down to the county of Charlotte and made the discovery that the oil had to come in barrels. I do not know what idea he had held previously. It had to come in some form from overseas, and the fact was that it came in thin, black metal barrels. The barrels were being sold to the fishermen at $1 each. I could buy all I wanted at that price. This gentleman from the department placed a value of $3 on the barrels and duty was collected accordingly.

Customs Act
That is what is meant when we refer to entering a wedge in any legislation of this kind. I wish to repeat emphatically that I believe we should move very carefully and, in so far as striking out the word "manufactured" is concerned, I would rather see it the way it is. I do not want to see the legislation broadened in any way. There is a specific purpose for which it was designed, and I am prepared to support that purpose. However, I wish to go on record today as opposing the broadening of the legislation in any way.
We are an exporting nation, and the last thing in the world we would want to see done by this government is anything that would indicate to the United States or to any other part of the world that we are not prepared to stand or fall on Liberal principles. For that reason I wish to go on record as supporting the suggestions put forth here today by the hon. member for Rosthern.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, speaking today the hon. member for Eglinton said that in his opinion this bill is too restrictive. He said it did not go far enough, as it applied only to manufactured goods. Thus he advocated that it should be broadened. Following this he introduced his amendment.
I understood this to be a specific measure to do a specific job. It is emergency legislation to benefit the textile industry. That was my understanding of it, and on that basis I supported it. In the earlier discussions that took place in the house it was suggested-and perhaps I urged this more fervently than anyone else, and over a longer period-that we needed this emergency legislation in order to meet a situation which has jeopardized the economy of a segment of our people, as well as their standard of living.
We started out to repair a break in the dike: now we are starting out to build a wall around the dike-and even a wall around the old wall. I think this is a mistake. It is a mistake to broaden this measure. There is something to be said for those of us who, over the years, have stood by Liberal principles. Sometimes those Liberal principles have hurt, even in my own riding. On the other hand if we start now to extend and broaden the scope of this bill we shall turn it into a protective tariff measure. That would be a mistake. I intend to vote against it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would hope that the government would see fit to adopt the amendment. However, I do find myself confused. Several hon. members have suggested that this measure is proposed for the benefit of only a certain group of individuals.

Yet, in the explanatory note, I see it says that the subsection is to supplement and to widen the law. However, there may be further explanations forthcoming from other hon. members indicating exactly what they mean. I am particularly interested in the suggestion that the measure should apply to end of season goods. In my remarks the other day I dealt particularly with potatoes. End of season goods coming into my part of the country applies not only to potatoes but also to fruits and vegetables. This is a most important matter, and one which should be considered.
I believe section 43 of the Customs Act is intended to look after the fruit farmers. However, I find that, as a whole, they are reaching the point where they need additional protection. For that reason I should like to see hon. members adopt the amendment proposed.
If the amendment is not accepted, then the government might see fit to adopt the idea of establishing an international commodity clearance house, and thus get rid of our surpluses.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of what the Prime Minister said, let me state that I am going to vote against the amendment, and I shall give my reasons for doing so. They are the reasons I set out when I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As reported at page 292 of Hansard, I said:
In the speech from the throne we also find the following reference to free trade-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: Order. I am sorry, but the hon. member cannot quote from a previous debate in the same session.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not have to quote it word for word. In the speech from the throne the government reaffirmed the Liberal principles of free trade, and I think we should stick to those Liberal principles. Any deviation from them should be kept as limited as possible.
Speaking the other day one hon. member opposite reproached Liberals for departing from the principle of free trade in this instance. Let me say to him that he should not throw stones when he lives in a glass house. Hon. members opposite have always been in favour of high protection and have always fought any measure introduced by a Liberal government to foster free trade between this great nation of ours and other nations in the world.
For the reasons I have given I am going to vote against the amendment.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot understand the arguments of those hon. members

Customs Act
who say they are not in favour of the amendment because they feel that the benefits, if any, that will follow from the legislation should be confined to manufactured goods.
It has always been my impression that it was the widespread belief of a large number of members in the house, particularly those from western Canada, that it was entirely unfair that the principle followed in matters of this kind should be protection for the manufacturers and competition for the farmers. It seems to me that the farmers of the west, particularly, are entitled to as much assistance in meeting their economic problems as manufacturers in any part of Canada.
Knowing as I do that our primary producers of fruits and vegetables are at the present time facing a serious problem of this sort, it does seem to me it would be only fair for hon. members to support the amendment of the hon. member for Eglinton. If the hon. member for Spadina will permit me, may I say I was interested in his reference which, as I recall it, went something like this. If there was a hole in the dike he felt that we should fix that hole or confine our attention to that hole alone, and not go about extending the dike. The hon. member will probably recall, as I do, the old story of the little Dutch boy-I think his name was Peter. He found a hole in a dike. He was a brave little boy, and he shoved his finger in. It is probable the hon. member will recall that the outcome of that story was not a happy one, because not only did the dike eventually become breached completely but Peter was drowned.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
As one who is in partnership
with the weather and the soil in manufacturing a commodity that has to be sold on the free markets of the world, namely, wheat, perhaps I might be permitted to say just a word on this. I can consider this legislation only in the light of an emergency. I can go further than that and say that if I am going to support it-I have not yet made up my mind-it will be because it will perhaps stop a sharp practice on the part of our United States friends.
If this committee passes the amendment of the hon. member for Eglinton it will widen the scope of this purely emergency measure. While I am on my feet I might say that I am entirely a free trader. I believe that one of the curses of the world is this matter of tariffs. I am afraid that in time this measure will become the thin edge of the wedge. As a matter of fact, only three quarters of an hour ago I could sense that, when the hon. member for Eglinton spoke. We are heading in the direction of protection that will eventually lead to a
world debacle such as we had in the early 1930's and that eventually culminated in war. I do not want to enlarge on that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext: It was 1929, to be exact.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I am speaking entirely on the
amendment. I hope that I get an opportunity some later time when I shall be able to remind the house of the disastrous effect of protection not only in this country but in every country of the world, culminating eventually in war.
Tariffs are one of the main reasons why we have war. I cannot go into detail now, but I will at some future time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
I have been listening to
the last two or three speakers and wondering really what we were talking about. I really admire your generosity, sir, in allowing the debate to stray as it has.
We are debating a bill brought in by this government with respect to the matter of dumping. Anti-dumping legislation, as the minister told us the other night, was originally introduced by a Liberal government in 1904. When the minister spoke the other night he was at pains, and quite properly so, to say that this legislation in no sense concerned tariffs in any way; that it was entirely within the scope of GATT to which we have adhered. Now we have attempts to hear the old song sung again, and hon. members are rising in their places and trying to distort, for example, the words used by my colleague, the hon. member for Eglinton, and suggest that they detect in it high-tariff proclivities, and we are somehow or other almost pictured as conspirators.
I should like to remind you that when trade matters were up in the house the last time, which, as I recall it, was the general agreement on tariffs and trade, we supported them. If anyone cares to know the facts, if he will look at the debates he will see that we supported that agreement, and have supported it throughout. I do hope, Mr. Chairman, that we will get the committee back to some degree of common sense, and not have this old, old story-my colleague the hon. member for Eglinton suggests "accuracy", and that is a useful addition- that we will not have any more of this nonsense talked. When we are trying to improve this legislation, which is supposed to guard against what has always been thought of as a really unfair and even almost dishonest method of competing, I do hope we will not have any more suggestions that we are dark tariff conspirators.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING MINISTER TO APPRAISE GOODS ON WEIGHTED AVERAGE
speechtext:
Is there any protection in
the Customs Act for vegetable growers or flower growers?
